lines: In the Star Door mystery, you learned that empty, quiet, blank and hidden do not mean the same as nothing. Careful words helped the team say exactly what they found.
At the end of that mystery, a hidden ramp delivered a parcel beside the five-star map. The same parcel is waiting in the library now, with Mia, Sol and Tavi written on its label.
Inside is a Moon Lantern. When it cannot fit through a small door, you will study the whole, separate its four parts, carry and count them, then build the same whole again.
Pax knows how things fit together. You do not need to know every new word yet. Try each puzzle, and after every game I will explain what your actions helped you learn.
The parcel that slid down the library ramp after the first mystery was waiting beside the five-star map.
There is the parcel, beside the map. The label says Mia, Sol and Tavi. It is for us! Help me move it along the glowing floor path to the yellow reading mat.

You moved the parcel one square at a time and followed the glowing path to its end. Following a route in order helps us reach the right place. Inside the parcel is a Moon Lantern, with a card asking the team to take it to the balcony.
The friends followed the card towards the balcony. A small door blocked the way. The lantern was too wide to fit through it.
Hello! I’m Pax. We can take the lantern apart, carry every part through, and build the whole lantern again. First, tap the covered lantern. Each tap will uncover one part.
You uncovered all four parts and saw one whole Moon Lantern. A whole has every part it needs, with no missing part and no extra object. Now the team knows exactly what they must rebuild.
The lantern came apart into four pieces. All four waited beside the small door.
The door is narrow, so we must carry one lantern part at a time. Let’s move all four through, and not carry any part twice.
You carried all four lantern parts through the small door. Each part moved once: none was missed and none was carried twice. Keeping track lets us know the complete set reached the other side.
Pax laid four lantern-picture cards beside a round plan frame.
Each card shows one same-size part. Match every curved part to its place. The four parts must fill the lantern plan with no gap and no part on top of another.

You matched each lantern part to its place. All four parts meet with no gap and no overlap. The finished plan has matching sides; that is called symmetrical. The four separate parts now show one whole lantern.
Mia placed the empty round frame on the balcony. The four parts they had counted waited beside it.
Our equation checked that all four parts are here. Now fit each part into the frame. Use every part once, and leave none behind.

You used each counted part once and rebuilt the whole Moon Lantern. The same four parts became one whole again. A blue moon lit up, then a gold sun. The two lights began to take turns, pointing towards the next adventure.
Pax put two pairs of lantern-part pictures on the balance table.
One pair shows lantern parts that are the same size. Look at both pairs before you choose.
Pair A stayed level because its two lantern parts are the same size. Pair B tipped because one part is bigger. This check teaches us to compare sizes instead of guessing from a quick look.
Pax placed three lantern-part pictures in a flat practice frame. One picture space was empty. Another lantern picture and a triangle were nearby.
Which picture completes the practice frame? Choose it, turn its top upright, and fit it into the empty space.

You turned the lantern picture upright and fitted it into the empty space. It filled the gap; the triangle and square were extra shapes, so they stayed outside. This teaches us that a whole needs the right parts in the right places.
Pax held two lantern parts. The other two waited on the tray, so all four were still easy to see.
How many parts am I holding? Then tell me how many parts make the whole lantern.
You counted two parts in Pax's hands and two on the tray. Two and two make four altogether. Counting both groups tells us that all four parts of the whole lantern are still here.
The friends reached the balcony before the first evening star. All four lantern parts were still separate, ready to be counted together.
Put one lantern part in each space. A plus sign means join the separate counts. The equals sign tells us the total on the other side must count the same parts.

One part plus one part plus one part plus one part equals four parts. Plus joins the separate counts. Equals tells us that both sides count the same four parts. The equation checks that every lantern part reached the balcony.

Here is what you learned. One whole can be made from several exact parts. You kept track of all four lantern parts, counted them with addition, and used the equals sign to show that both sides named the same total. Then you fitted those four parts together to rebuild one whole. This matters because counting and a clear parts plan help us check that nothing has been missed or used twice.
